findings.claim: All 60 practice questions, and the exam tips in lessons 1, 2, 4, 6 and 8, use another board's forms: '2 marks - Describe One Feature', '4 marks - Describe Two Features', '8 marks - Explain Causation', '16 marks - Significance Question', '5 marks - Historic Environment Explain'. Lesson 8's exam tip names a 5-mark site question.
findings.truth: This paper runs 1 hour 15 minutes for 55 marks in two sections. The depth study is worth 35 marks: an 'Explain...' question for 10 marks (AO1 5 + AO2 5) and an essay using sources for 25 marks (AO1 5, AO2 5, AO3 10, SPaG 5). The site study is worth 20 marks: an 'Explain...' question for 10 marks and a source comparison for 10 marks, with no SPaG. AO4 carries zero marks here, so there is no interpretation question, and no Describe form and no 2-, 4-, 5-, 8- or 16-mark question exists on this paper.
findings.evidence: specs/ocr/history-a-J410.md - component overview table (55 marks, 1 hour 15 minutes) and the component group 3 assessment tables: 'The British depth study will be assessed by two questions' and 'The study of the historic environment will be assessed by two questions'.

findings.claim: 'In Scotland, a separate Jacobite uprising at Killiecrankie (1689) was defeated.'
findings.truth: Killiecrankie (27 July 1689) was a Jacobite victory over the Williamite army. Their commander Viscount Dundee was killed in the battle, and the rising then collapsed, losing at Dunkeld in August 1689 and Cromdale in 1690.
findings.evidence: Lesson 3 of this same unit states the correct outcome: 'Jacobite forces under Bonnie Dundee routed a Williamite army, though Dundee was killed in the moment of victory.'

findings.claim: 'Parliament offered the throne jointly to William and Mary in February 1689. Before they were crowned, they had to accept the Bill of Rights (December 1689).' The conclusion repeats it: 'William and Mary were jointly crowned in February 1689 on condition of accepting the Bill of Rights.'
findings.truth: What William and Mary accepted on 13 February 1689 was the Declaration of Right. They were crowned on 11 April 1689. Parliament only enacted the Bill of Rights in December 1689, after the coronation, so it cannot have been the condition of it. The dates given are individually right but the sequence is impossible.
findings.evidence: Standard constitutional chronology: Declaration of Right February 1689, coronation April 1689, Bill of Rights December 1689.

findings.claim: The Wild Geese departure is called 'one of the largest forced emigrations in Irish history'.
findings.truth: The Treaty of Limerick offered the Jacobite army the choice of leaving for France, and about 12,000 to 14,000 took it. It was exile by agreement, not transportation. This option asks students to distinguish voluntary emigration, indentured labour and forced emigration, so blurring the categories costs precision marks.
findings.evidence: spec 2, Impact of Empire content: 'Emigration (including forced emigration) from the British Isles to the Americas'; the lesson's own account of the treaty terms.

findings.claim: 'Many Irish Catholics settled in Catholic Maryland and in the Caribbean colonies.'
findings.truth: Maryland was founded as a Catholic refuge, but Catholic government there ended with the Protestant Revolution of 1689. It became a royal colony in 1692, the Church of England was established the same year, and Catholic worship was restricted from 1704. For 1688-c.1730 'Catholic Maryland' misdescribes the destination.
findings.evidence: Chronology of the Maryland Protestant Revolution 1689 and the 1704 Act against Catholic worship.

findings.claim: 'The Calico Acts (1690 and 1720) attempted to restrict Indian textile imports.' The date pair also appears in flashcard 7 and in the knowledge-check matching options ('1720').
findings.truth: There was no Calico Act in 1690. The first was passed in 1700 and the second received royal assent on 23 March 1721. Both dates in the lesson are wrong, and the wrong second date is baked into an answer key.
findings.evidence: Wikipedia 'Calico Acts': the Acts were passed in 1700 and 1721 (the second is formally titled 'Woollen, etc., Manufactures Act 1720' but assented 23 March 1721).

findings.claim: 'The EIC held a royal monopoly on English trade with Asia; its monopoly was renewed by Parliament in 1700.' The claim is repeated in the mark scheme for practice question 6.
findings.truth: Parliament did the opposite. In 1698 it chartered a rival English Company Trading to the East Indies in return for a two million pound loan, breaking the old company's exclusive right. The two companies competed until they merged in 1709. Nothing was renewed in 1700.
findings.evidence: East India Company Act 1698; the united company of 1709.

findings.claim: Five exam tips assert what examiners do: 'examiners reward precise terminology' (L4), 'Examiners reward answers that show how these developments reinforced each other' (L5), 'examiners expect you to use accurate terminology... will be marked down at higher levels' (L6), 'Examiners at the highest level expect you to show contradictions... exactly what the highest-band answers do' (L7), 'Examiners reward judgements about purpose and limitation' (L10).
findings.truth: None of these is sourced from anything. They are invented examiner claims of the kind the fact-check gate exists to remove. The underlying advice is sound and has been kept, rephrased as advice rather than as a report of examiner behaviour.
findings.evidence: House rule on fabricated examiner claims.

findings.claim: Flashcard 4 answer: 'Silk textiles (including calicoes and muslins)'.
findings.truth: Calico and muslin are cotton cloths. The East India Company's famous and politically explosive Indian import was cotton, which is exactly why English wool weavers petitioned Parliament and the Calico Acts followed. The answer key taught the wrong fibre.
findings.evidence: spec 2, Economic impact of empire: 'growing trade with India and China'; the lesson's own text names calicoes and muslins alongside the weavers' petitions.

findings.claim: Key fact: 470,000 enslaved Africans carried by British ships 1700-1730 was 'around three times the RAC's total in the previous thirty years'.
findings.truth: The lesson itself puts the RAC's total at an estimated 100,000 across 1672-1713. 470,000 against 100,000 is nearly five times, over roughly forty years, not three times over thirty. The arithmetic contradicts the lesson's own figures.
findings.evidence: Internal inconsistency with the figures given two paragraphs earlier.

findings.claim: 'the South Sea Company's mismanagement of the contract caused the South Sea Bubble crash of 1720.'
findings.truth: The crash came from the 1720 scheme in which the company took on government debt in exchange for its own shares, and from the speculation that scheme set off. The Asiento was a disappointment, but it did not cause the bubble. The lesson's own content section gives the correct cause, so the takeaway contradicts the teaching.
findings.evidence: The lesson's own collapsible on the South Sea Bubble.

findings.claim: 'Individual writers such as Mary Astell commented critically on the contradictions of a society that celebrated liberty while enslaving others.' Flashcard 8 answers 'Mary Astell'.
findings.truth: Mary Astell (1666-1731) wrote about the position of women. Her famous line - if all men are born free, how is it that all women are born slaves - is from Some Reflections upon Marriage and uses slavery as a metaphor for marriage. She wrote nothing against the Atlantic slave trade. Genuine in-period examples exist: Aphra Behn's Oroonoko (1688) and the Quaker Thomas Tryon's attacks on planters in the 1680s.
findings.evidence: Mary Astell's published works; Behn, Oroonoko (1688).

findings.claim: 'Equiano's earlier life overlapped with the world of the coffee houses and shows that the enslaved diaspora had a presence and a voice in British cities' in 1688-c.1730.
findings.truth: Olaudah Equiano was born about 1745 and bought his freedom in 1766. No part of his life falls inside 1688-c.1730. The lesson already flags his 1789 book as too late, then uses him as evidence anyway. A student who cites him for this option is writing outside its dates.
findings.evidence: spec 2: the option is dated 1688-c.1730.

findings.claim: 'The community built the Christ Church Spitalfields, designed by Nicholas Hawksmoor and completed in 1729 (not 1743 as sometimes cited).'
findings.truth: Christ Church was a state church, not a community one. Parliament funded it from the coal duty under the 1711 Act for Fifty New Churches, and it was placed in Spitalfields partly to assert the Church of England in a district full of foreign Protestants and dissenters. That is also what makes it useful evidence about how the settled authorities received migrants.
findings.evidence: The Fifty New Churches Act 1711; spec, Urban Environments: 'Positive and negative responses by the authorities'.

findings.claim: 'The most important single building in the historic environment examination is...'; 'Examiners consistently reward students who can name all four uses and their approximate dates'; 'This is the single most tested piece of Spitalfields evidence.'
findings.truth: Three invented claims about what the examination tests and rewards. The building genuinely is the richest single piece of evidence on the site, so the teaching point stands once the invented exam claims are stripped out.
findings.evidence: House rule on fabricated examiner and exam-paper claims.

findings.claim: 'By 1714, the national debt stood at around 54 million pounds.'
findings.truth: Two readings. (a) The figure is wrong for 1714: the usual figure for the debt at the end of the War of the Spanish Succession is roughly 36 to 40 million pounds, and about 54 million is the level reached around 1720 after the South Sea debt conversion - so change to 'around 36 million'. (b) The figure is defensible if it includes unfunded debt and arrears, which some tables do. I could not verify either value: the Wikipedia article on the British national debt gives no figure between 1694 and 1815. RECOMMENDATION: change to 'around 40 million pounds', which every standard table supports, rather than leave a figure that matches 1720.
findings.evidence: WebFetch of Wikipedia 'History of the British national debt' returned no figure for 1697, 1714 or 1720; WebSearch budget exhausted.

findings.claim: 'In 1698, the Company established a factory (trading post) at Kolkata (Calcutta).' The date is repeated in a key fact, a knowledge check, a flashcard, the conclusion and two mark schemes.
findings.truth: Two defensible dates. Job Charnock settled at Sutanuti in 1690, which many textbooks call the founding of Calcutta; in 1698 the Company bought the zamindari rights of the three villages and began Fort William, which is the date the lesson uses. The spec names 'the establishment in Kolkata' without a year, so neither is wrong against the spec, and changing it would ripple through six fields. RECOMMENDATION: keep 1698 and add one clause to the content noting the 1690 settlement, leaving every answer key untouched.
findings.evidence: spec 2, Economic impact of empire: 'growing trade with India and China and the establishment in Kolkata and role of the East India Company'.

findings.claim: 'Around 50,000 Huguenots fled to England over the following years; perhaps 13,000 to 15,000 settled in London.' Repeated in a key fact, a flashcard and the conclusion.
findings.truth: The 50,000 total for England is standard. The London figure is not: the usual estimate is that about half of the refugees, roughly 25,000, settled in London, while 13,000 to 15,000 is closer to the figure usually given for Spitalfields itself. Either the number is too low or the place is wrong. RECOMMENDATION: change 'settled in London' to 'settled in Spitalfields', which keeps the number, keeps the flashcard answer usable and makes the sentence true. I could not verify the London figure - the Wikipedia Huguenots article gives no English or London breakdown.
findings.evidence: WebFetch of Wikipedia 'Huguenots' returned only a 200,000-1,000,000 total for all destinations; WebSearch budget exhausted.

findings.claim: 'Seven leading English nobles wrote to William of Orange.'
findings.truth: The Immortal Seven included Bishop Compton of London and two commoners, Edward Russell and Henry Sidney. 'Seven leading Englishmen' would be safer, but no mark rides on it.
findings.evidence: checker judgement; not verified further

findings.claim: 'Seamas an Caca' glossed as 'James the Coward'.
findings.truth: The Irish is 'Seamas an Chaca'; 'caca' as written means cake. The usual translation is blunter than 'coward'. No exam mark depends on the Irish spelling.
findings.evidence: checker judgement; not verified further

findings.claim: 'James fled to France the following day' after the Boyne.
findings.truth: James reached Dublin on the evening of 1 July 1690, left Dublin on 2 July and sailed from Kinsale on 4 July. He began his flight the following day; he did not reach France then.
findings.evidence: checker judgement; not verified further

findings.claim: 'around 12,000 Irish soldiers left for France' as the Wild Geese.
findings.truth: Most estimates put the Flight of the Wild Geese at about 14,000 soldiers, though 12,000 is widely printed. The figure is repeated in lesson 4 and in three answer keys, so it is not worth moving on a contested number.
findings.evidence: checker judgement; not verified further

findings.claim: 'Political transportation began with Cromwell.'
findings.truth: Transportation of convicts to the colonies was already in use from about 1615 under James I. Cromwell's shipments of Irish and Scottish prisoners in the 1650s were a large escalation, not the start.
findings.evidence: checker judgement; not verified further

findings.claim: 'By c.1720 the EIC was importing millions of pounds of tea per year.'
findings.truth: Legal tea imports reached roughly a million pounds a year in the 1720s and only ran into several millions by the 1750s, so 'millions' looks about a decade early. I could not verify a figure, so no edit.
findings.evidence: checker judgement; not verified further

findings.claim: 'the cutting season ran for most of the year'.
findings.truth: The Caribbean sugar crop season ran roughly January to June. The point being made - punishing, sustained labour - survives without the overstatement.
findings.evidence: checker judgement; not verified further

findings.claim: The lesson dates the South Sea Bubble to 1720; the spec prints 1719.
findings.truth: 1720 is the correct history and is what every answer key here uses. The spec's 1719 refers to the year the scheme was proposed. No change: a student writing 1720 is right.
findings.evidence: checker judgement; not verified further

findings.claim: 'By 1700, London had over 2,000 coffee houses.'
findings.truth: This is the standard textbook figure and would be credited, but historians of the coffee house put the real number in the hundreds; licence records show about 550 in 1739. It is repeated in a key fact, a knowledge check, a flashcard and the conclusion, so it is not worth moving on a contested number.
findings.evidence: checker judgement; not verified further

findings.claim: '"Mauvillain" became "Mowbray"' as a Huguenot anglicisation.
findings.truth: I could not verify this specific pair. Well-attested examples exist (Blanc to White, Boileau to Drinkwater). Worth checking before it is quoted in a lesson.
findings.evidence: checker judgement; not verified further

findings.claim: Lesson descriptions in lessons 7, 8, 9 and 10 run to 101, 109, 106 and 115 characters.
findings.truth: The validator limit is under 100 characters, so the unit would be rejected on write. Each has been trimmed below the limit with its meaning intact.
findings.evidence: CHECK_PROMPT_HISTORY.md validator limits.

summary: Every practice label in the unit came from another board: 2/4/8/16-mark Describe, Explain Causation and Significance forms, plus a 5-mark site question. This paper sets four questions only - a 10-mark explain and a 25-mark essay using sources on the depth study, a 10-mark explain and a 10-mark source comparison on Spitalfields - so all 60 questions were relabelled and the Describe stems rewritten as explain, essay or comparison tasks. Content errors: Killiecrankie called a Jacobite defeat when it was a Jacobite victory (L1, and lesson 3 says so), the Bill of Rights made the condition of a coronation eight months before it existed (L1), Calico Acts dated 1690 and 1720 instead of 1700 and 1721 (L5, with the wrong date in an answer key), the East India Company monopoly said to be renewed in 1700 when Parliament broke it in 1698 (L5), calicoes and muslins called silk in a flashcard answer (L5), Mary Astell presented as a critic of Atlantic slavery when she wrote about marriage (L7), and Equiano, born about 1745, used as evidence for 1688-c.1730 (L7). Five exam tips invented examiner behaviour and three claims invented what the site paper tests most. Lessons 3 and 9 were clean of content errors.
